desc:
Encoding. The array nxt describes a successor function on the positions 0..n-1: from position i a step always leads to position nxt[i].

For every position s, imagine a walker that starts at s and takes steps along nxt for ever. Let ans[s] be the number of different positions the walker visits, counting s itself.

Return the array ans of length n.

Example: nxt = [1,2,0,2,3]. Position 0 visits 0,1,2 (3 positions), position 3 visits 3,2,0,1 (4), position 4 visits 4,3,2,0,1 (5), so the answer is [3,3,3,4,5]. A position with nxt[i] = i only visits itself, so its value is 1.
hints: Walking from every start separately with a visited set costs O(n<sup>2</sup>) in the worst case. The answers of different starts are strongly related.
A position on a cycle visits exactly the cycle, so its answer is the cycle length. A position off the cycle visits itself plus everything its successor visits: ans[i] = 1 + ans[nxt[i]].

Walk from each unfinished start, recording the path. If the walk runs into the path itself, the closed part is a new cycle: give all of its positions the cycle length. Then fill the rest of the path backwards using ans[i] = 1 + ans[nxt[i]]. Positions that are already finished stop a walk immediately.
editorial: Every position has one outgoing step, so each walk is a tail that leads into a cycle (the 'rho' shape). The number of distinct positions visited is tail length plus cycle length, and for cycle positions it is just the cycle length.

Use states: 0 unseen, 1 on the current path, 2 finished. For an unfinished start, follow nxt and push positions on a path until you reach a position that is not state 0. If that position is on the current path (state 1) at index j, the positions path[j:] form a cycle of length len(path) - j: set their answer to it and mark them finished. Whatever remains in the path before the cycle (or the whole path, if you stopped on a finished position) is processed from the end backwards with ans[v] = ans[nxt[v]] + 1. Each position enters a path exactly once, so the algorithm is O(n) time and O(n) memory. The cycle detection can use Floyd's slow/fast pointers instead of the state array, but the path-recording variant gives all answers in one sweep.
solution:
def visitedCounts(nxt):
    n = len(nxt)
    ans = [0] * n
    state = [0] * n  # 0 unseen, 1 on current path, 2 finished
    for s in range(n):
        if state[s]:
            continue
        path = []
        u = s
        while state[u] == 0:
            state[u] = 1
            path.append(u)
            u = nxt[u]
        if state[u] == 1:
            j = path.index(u)
            c = len(path) - j
            for v in path[j:]:
                ans[v] = c
                state[v] = 2
            del path[j:]
        for v in reversed(path):
            ans[v] = ans[nxt[v]] + 1
            state[v] = 2
    return ans
